subject: A potential scalability issue in my model

messages.author: f42b0240615306ac
messages.subject: A potential scalability issue in my model
parts:
Hi, 

I have a mixed linear model as follow:

y = X * beta + u + e
u ~ N(0, a * K)
e ~ N(0, b * I)

Here covariance matrix K is known. Cholesky decomposition was applied on K as follow:

L = chol(K)
u = L * z
z ~ N(0, 1)

Here z is a vector in the parameter block, u was defined as transformed parameter, major parts of the model would be:

parameters {
  real<lower=machine_precision()> a;
  real<lower=machine_precision()> b;
  vector[N] z;
}

transformed parameters{
  vector[N] u;
  u <- a * L * z;
}

model {
  z ~ normal(0, 1);
  y ~ normal(mu + u, b);
}

My question is on parameter "a", which is the scale factor of the covariance matrix. 
It seems unnecessary but only make scalability issue given z will be estimated and "a" is only a scale factor of z. Can I comfortably take it off from the model?

Also, I found including "a" often made the model estimations unstable.

Xulong

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A potential scalability issue in my model
parts:
Would you mind sending the data block? It makes it easier than
me having to reverse engineer data shapes and sizes.

I'm confused by this:
> y ~ normal(mu + u, b);

because u is a scaled Cholesky factor, which isn't a legal
argument in that place on the normal, I don't think.

And if you want to fit a scale you obviously need to declare it
as a parameter.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A potential scalability issue in my model
parts:
Thanks. That helps. But it's still even easier if you
just give us the whole program in one big block. It's hard
for a second person to come in and piece it all back together.
But I think I see what you're doing now.
> Given my model: y = X * beta + u + e, I wrote: y ~ normal(mu + u, b); why is this not appropriate?

Yes, that's appropriate. I was just lost in the types. I now see
you're multiplying L by a vector to get a vector u.

I think you should probably declare L as

cholesky_factor_cov[N] L;

That will makes sure that L really is a Cholesky factor for
a positive-definite matrix. And it'll make the intent of your
program easier for others to follow.

Or you could take in the covariance matrix and do the cholesky
factoring in the transformed data block. It only gets run once
as the data is read in.

I still don't understand why you'd want to add a scale term.
Isn't the covariance matrix already scaled? What we often do
is work in terms of a scaled correlation matrix.

In general, multiplying two parameters can be problematic
because it introduces a multiplicative non-identifiability, which
even with priors, tends to lead to a banana-shaped posterior.
This is bad news because the posterior covariance then isn't
position independent, and therefore Stan's HMC algorithms can't
find good global step sizes and mass matrices for jumping --- they
just have to take something very small, which is costly in log
density evaluations.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A potential scalability issue in my model
parts:
> On Oct 23, 2015, at 3:43 PM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I still don't understand why you'd want to add a scale term.
> Isn't the covariance matrix already scaled? What we often do
> is work in terms of a scaled correlation matrix.
>
> The covariance matrix was already scaled. The intention to put the scale factor was to scale the actual values of the random variables u, while u ~ L * z. While cov(u) ~ L, I thought there might be an additional scale on u for its real effect on the response, just like the parameter of another fixed predictor.
>
> Almost certain this is unnecessary, because the estimation of z will automatically give u in the right scale, given y. Please let me know if I miss anything.

That's right. You should only provide one place
for the scale to get estimated or you get multiplied parameters,
which leads to very weakly identified posteriors shaped like
bananas which are bad news for sampling.

- Bob
